title: IdentityHashMap: reference equality (==) instead of equals()
keyPoints: IdentityHashMap uses reference equality (==) for key comparison instead of equals(), and System.identityHashCode() instead of hashCode().
Two objects with identical content but different memory addresses are treated as different keys.
It intentionally violates the general Map contract, which specifies equals-based key comparison.
Internally it uses a flat Object array with linear probing, not a bucket-and-chain structure.
Common use cases include serialization graphs, deep-copy tracking, cycle detection, and JVM internals.
String literals that are interned to the same reference collapse to one key, unlike new String() instances.
IdentityHashMap is not synchronised and is a special-purpose class that should not be used as a general-purpose Map.

s1_definition.oneliner: IdentityHashMap uses reference equality (==) instead of equals() for key comparison, so two distinct objects with the same content are treated as two different keys.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Reference equality** – keys are compared with `==` (same object in memory), not `equals()` (same content)
- **System.identityHashCode()** – the hash is computed from the object's memory identity, not from the overridden `hashCode()` method
- **Flat array with linear probing** – internally stores keys and values in alternating slots of a single `Object[]`, not in Node buckets
- **Intentional contract violation** – the Javadoc explicitly states this class violates the Map contract by design
- **Special-purpose only** – meant for scenarios where object identity matters, such as serialization, deep copy, and topology-preserving transformations
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, each physical cheque is a unique piece of paper. A normal HashMap treats two cheques with the same account number SAV2001 as one key because the content matches. An IdentityHashMap treats each physical cheque as a separate key, even if both carry the same account number. You care about which specific piece of paper, not what is written on it. This is useful when Rajesh's serialization service needs to track which exact Java objects have already been serialized to avoid writing the same object twice.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  HashMap vs IdentityHashMap Key Comparison
  ==========================================

  Two String objects: key1 = new String("SAV2001")
                      key2 = new String("SAV2001")

  HashMap:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ key1.equals(key2) -> true          │
  │ key1.hashCode() == key2.hashCode() │
  │ Result: SAME key, value replaced   │
  └────────────────────────────────────┘

  IdentityHashMap:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ key1 == key2 -> false (different objects in memory)    │
  │ System.identityHashCode(key1) != identityHashCode(key2)│
  │ Result: TWO different keys                             │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Internal storage (flat array, linear probing):
  ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
  │k1 │v1 │   │   │k2 │v2 │   │   │
  └───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘
   [0] [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7]
   key val       key val
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
IdentityHashMap is a special-purpose Map that uses reference equality (==) and System.identityHashCode() instead of equals() and hashCode(). Two objects with identical content but different memory addresses are treated as two separate keys. This intentional violation of the Map contract serves scenarios where object identity matters more than content equality.

The classic use case is tracking objects during serialization or deep copy. When Rajesh's deep-copy service at National Bank of India clones a complex loan application graph, it uses an IdentityHashMap to record which exact objects have already been cloned. Two LoanApplication objects with the same loan ID but different instance addresses are correctly treated as separate entities.

Internally, IdentityHashMap uses a flat Object array with linear probing instead of the bucket-chain structure of HashMap. This makes it more cache-friendly for small maps but less efficient under high load due to clustering. Watch out for interning: String literals and cached Integers (-128 to 127) share references, so they collapse to a single key even in an IdentityHashMap.

Remember one sentence: IdentityHashMap compares keys with == instead of equals(), treating every distinct object as a separate key, which is essential for serialization graphs and cycle detection but wrong for general-purpose maps.
